reader: AI reader 15 (targeted check at the stated place, PDFs)

results.note: Every number matches. 2.2 (p. 2): search to 15 June 2020, no language limit. 3.1 and 3.2 (p. 3): six trials, 395 people, all head-to-head; arms 129, 93, 48, 60, 36 and 29 (sum 395). Table 1 (p. 4): 21 to 42 days; two trials each in Thailand, Iran and China; Leelahanaj outpatient, the other five inpatient; per-trial totals 56, 53, 80, 44, 42 and 120 (editors' sums reproduced, 42 to 120; 29 + 27 = 56). The Leelahanaj 2005 and Farnia 2014 reference entries, whose titles name amphetamine psychosis, are on p. 8; p. 7 holds only the first two reference entries. The anchor names the Wang 2020 pair as paliperidone vs risperidone, as Table 1, Fig. 2A and Fig. 3A do; the 3.2 text names aripiprazole (a reporting issue already on the card). Role supports: right.

3.5 (p. 5): no significant difference on main symptoms in all six trials, on positive symptoms in four, on negative symptoms in three; dropout not compared statistically in five. Matches. Role supports.

Fig. 3A read on p. 5 rendered at 250 dpi: olanzapine −1.09 (−1.89; −0.28) and quetiapine −0.86 (−1.61; −0.11), 0 direct comparisons; haloperidol −0.60 (−1.20; 0.01) and paliperidone −0.33 (−0.69; 0.03), 1 each; aripiprazole 0.27 (−0.13; 0.68), 2; legend I² 0%. Table 2A (p. 6) and Table 3 (p. 7): aripiprazole against olanzapine 1.36, quetiapine 1.13, haloperidol 0.87 and paliperidone 0.60 with the stated intervals, indirect, rated Low; the five direct estimates all Very low, every interval including 0. The 3.6 text (2nd paragraph) prints quetiapine as 0.86. Context for the claim: the network has no closed loop (6 trials, 5 basic comparisons), so the global I² rests on one degree of freedom, the two aripiprazole–risperidone trials, and 0% says nothing about consistency across the network (editors' reasoning). Role supports.

3.4 (p. 5): Samiei 2016 and Wang 2016 open-label, high risk in two domains; concealment not explicit in four; none found in Verachai 2014 and Wang 2020. 3.9 (p. 6): start high; risk of bias for results involving aripiprazole, haloperidol and risperidone because of the Samiei and Wang data; indirectness (intransitivity) for every outcome; imprecision where the interval crosses no effect; 2nd paragraph: all main-symptom estimates low or very low. Table 3 footnote letters agree (comparisons among olanzapine, paliperidone and quetiapine carry no risk-of-bias letter). Role qualifies.

The paper says 'a preferred', not 'the preferred' (p. 1; p. 7, 5th discussion paragraph); the quotation itself is verbatim (10 words). Arithmetic recomputed from the upper triangle of Table 2A: −0.49 + (−0.60) = −1.09 and −0.26 + (−0.60) = −0.86, as stated; Fig. 2A and the direct-comparison column of Fig. 3A (0, 0, 1, 1, 2) show a tree with no closed loop; Samiei is one of the two open-label trials (3.4) with 22 and 22 participants (Table 1). Role qualifies.
results.corrected_extracted: The authors conclude, while rating the evidence low quality, that olanzapine or quetiapine may be a preferred antipsychotic (abstract and last discussion paragraph). Editors' arithmetic from Table 2A and Fig. 3A: the direct comparisons form a chain without a closed loop, so indirect estimates are sums of single-trial estimates (olanzapine vs risperidone −1.09 = olanzapine vs haloperidol −0.49 plus haloperidol vs risperidone −0.60; quetiapine vs risperidone −0.86 = −0.26 plus −0.60), and both advantages over risperidone rest on the one open-label haloperidol–risperidone trial (Samiei 2016, 22 and 22 participants).

results.note: Values match: Fig. 1, read on the rendered page, gives the exclusion of one trial whose participants were less than mildly psychotic (mean PANSS total 51.6); 3.1 calls it an 8-week trial in people who had recovered; Fig. 3C (250 dpi) gives odds ratios from 0.18 (0.00; 50.14) for olanzapine to 2.77 (0.32; 23.95) for aripiprazole, none significant, I² 72.5% (legend; 3.7); the 3rd discussion paragraph lists the lack of any placebo control. That Sulaiman 2013 was placebo-controlled and tested aripiprazole is stated only in its reference title (p. 8), so that page is added. 'The one placebo-controlled trial found' holds for the ten full texts assessed. Role qualifies.
results.corrected_locator: 3.1, 1st paragraph and Fig. 1 (p. 3); 3.6, 4th paragraph and Fig. 3C (p. 5); 4. Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 6); reference list, Sulaiman et al. 2013 (p. 8)

results.note: Table 2 (p. 6): OR 1.88 (1.55–2.30), 2.14 (1.70–2.71), 1.33 (1.03–1.72); IRR 1.50 (1.26–1.78), 1.52 (1.26–1.85), 1.24 (1.02–1.50). Numbered point 2 (p. 4): p = 0.033 and 0.030. Time-dynamic covariates (p. 3) as listed. The text calls the fully adjusted model Model 3 and Table 2 calls it Model 2. Role supports.

Table 3 (p. 7): never 747 (71.9%); once or twice 124, 1.37 (0.86–2.17); less than or about monthly 117, 1.32 (0.82–2.11); at least weekly 51 (4.9%), 2.85 (1.21–6.69), p = 0.016; footnote: Model 1 fixed confounders only. The dose–response paragraph (p. 6) lists those covariates and gives p = 0.18 and 0.25 for the lower categories. Context for the claim: the categories are not monotonic (1.37, then 1.32), so this is a contrast resting on 51 people rather than a gradient; Table 3's heading says ages 18–35, the text 16–35. Role qualifies.

p. 2: exposure was asked for the period since the previous wave (16–18 to 30–35); symptoms for the past month at ages 18, 21 and 25 and since the previous assessment only at 30 and 35. 'For the same period at each interview' therefore holds only for the last two waves (the abstract describes both as covering the period since the previous interview, which the Methods contradict). Table 1 (p. 4) and the 5th discussion paragraph (p. 7) match. Role qualifies.
results.corrected_extracted: Use and symptoms were self-reported at the same interviews, over different windows at the first three: use of methamphetamine or other amphetamine-type stimulants (the question named speed, P and ice) since the previous interview at every wave; psychotic symptom items from the SCL-90 for the past month at ages 18, 21 and 25, and from the Diagnostic Interview Schedule for the period since the previous assessment at 30 and 35 (the authors say the difference in time frames was corrected in the analyses, without saying how); 35.2%, 41.8% and 36.4% reported at least one symptom in the periods to age 25; the authors note that some SCL-90 items arguably do not capture genuine psychotic experiences.

results.note: Numbers and the quotation (verbatim, 13 words) match pp. 4, 6 and 7. 'Assuming causality' is in the Methods' PAF paragraph (p. 3), not the Results' PAF paragraph, so p. 3 is added; 'for the same periods as use' changed for the reason given under n = 14. Role qualifies.
results.corrected_locator: Methods › Population attributable fraction (PAF) estimate (p. 3); Results › numbered point 4 (p. 4); Estimate of the population attributable fraction (p. 6); Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 7)
results.corrected_extracted: E-value 1.571 (confidence limit 1.11) for unmeasured confounding; population attributable fraction 8.0% (2.2%–14.7%), which the methods define as assuming causality. The authors conclude that methamphetamine use is an independent risk factor for psychosis in the general population, on self-reported symptom items reported at the same interviews as use.

results.note: 1st paragraph (p. 6): 27 studies (12 case-control, 5 cross-sectional, 4 longitudinal, 6 experimental), overall median 25%, no persistence in experimental studies, longest time to abate 12 h to 7 days, longitudinal median 40% (14–96%): all match. The case-report figure (24 case studies with duration data, persistence in two participants, 8%) is in the 3rd paragraph. Role supports.
results.corrected_locator: Results › Duration of symptoms, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

results.note: 2nd paragraph of Duration of symptoms (p. 6): Japan 41% (k = 11), median 44% (18–96%); 12% (0–39%) in fourteen studies from the USA, Australia, Canada, Iran and broader Asia; t = 4.79, p = .0001; ICD-10 35% vs DSM-IV 25% in Japanese studies, 6% vs 42% elsewhere. Discussion › Duration of psychotic symptoms, 1st paragraph (starts p. 7, ends p. 8): the Japanese excess is tied, in a relative clause, to those studies typically using the ICD, under which a primary psychotic disorder is diagnosed only after 6 months; 'attributes' is a fair reading. The review's own figures show ICD-10 in only about a third of the Japanese studies, which the anchor already gives. Role qualifies.

2nd paragraph of Longitudinal changes in symptom profile (p. 7): three studies; Kittirattanapaiboon 2010 (k = 1116) and Medhus 2015 (k = 28), 33–38% re-diagnosed after 6–7 years; a study of 825 patients, 16% within 16 years (Niemi-Pynttäri 2013). Matches, including the use of k for people. Role supports.

1st paragraph (starts p. 6, ends p. 7): four studies (Yeh 2001, Tomiyama 1990, Sato 1983, Javadian 2016); positive symptoms fell in three and were stable in one, negative symptoms stable in three and rose in one (Tomiyama: abstinent inpatients prescribed antipsychotics, 4 months); Javadian: 3-month follow-up, positive symptoms rose in those who used methamphetamine again. Matches. Role supports.

p. 2: 104 psychiatric inpatients with amphetamine delusional disorder (the DSM-III-R equivalent) who did not meet criteria for schizophrenia; 27% beyond one month and 17% beyond three months despite abstinence and antipsychotic treatment: matches. The Japanese hospital setting comes from the reference title on p. 10, outside the stated place, so that page is added. Role supports.
results.corrected_locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 2); reference list, Iwanami et al. 1994 (p. 10)

results.note: p. 4: 72% of studies recruited in- or outpatients from hospitals or psychiatric units. p. 8: no adjustment in many studies for polydrug use, frequency and duration of use or antipsychotic medication (1st paragraph), inpatient samples (2nd), no study of duration in community samples (3rd, continuing on p. 9). p. 9: binary coding cannot give prevalence; studies of differing quality aggregated without weighting (e.g. by sample size). 'No quality appraisal was made' is an inference from the methods, which describe none; it could be labelled as the editors' reading. Role qualifies.

Abstract (p. 182): 624 and 524; 3.2, 1st paragraph (p. 184): 527 and 624, 1151 in all, and the Table 1 group sizes sum to 624 and 527 (editors' check); 2.3 (p. 183): PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO to 16 December 2022; 3.1: 6 cross-sectional (two with a case-control design), 3 case-control, 2 cohort, 1 prospective; 3.2: Japan 3, Taiwan 2, Australia 2, China, Iran, Canada, South Africa 1 each, one study across four countries; mainly outpatients, 5 studies with in- and outpatients, 5 specifying a stability period. All match; countries and settings are in 3.2, not in Table 1. Role supports.

3.3.2, 3rd paragraph: −0.35 (−0.54 to −0.16), I² 54%. Fig. 2 read at 300 dpi: five study intervals exclude 0 (Mikami, Hajebi, Dawe, Chen, Wang); re-pooling its twelve values reproduces −0.35 (−0.54; −0.16), I² 54%. 3.5 (pp. 186–187): −0.44 (−0.82 to −0.07), p = 0.04. 3.3.2, 4th paragraph: leave-one-out −0.254 (−0.37 to −0.13), I² 58.0%. The paper does not name the omitted study; Mikami is the flagged outlier. Omitting Mikami from the Fig. 2 values gives −0.25 (−0.38 to −0.13) with a common-effect model and −0.28 (−0.44 to −0.12), I² 30%, with random effects (editors' calculation): the printed estimate fits a common-effect leave-one-out, the printed I² does not fit omitting Mikami. The anchor gives the printed values correctly. Role supports.

Recomputed: with the Dawe and Hajebi dispersions multiplied by the square root of n I get exactly −0.29 (−0.67; 0.10), tau² 0.40, I² 89%, studies from −1.93 (Mikami) to 0.54 (Srisurapanont); with Table 1 as printed, −0.35 (−0.90; 0.20), I² 94%. The anchor's 'from the means and SDs in Table 1' omits the standard-error reading, which the card states (key finding 4, reporting issue 3). Fig. 1 (300 dpi): study values −0.19 to 0.15, Mikami −0.04 (−0.49; 0.42); re-pooling the Fig. 1 values gives −0.01 (−0.13; 0.11), I² 0%, so the fault lies in the study-level inputs, not the pooling. The quotation is verbatim (3.3.1, 3rd paragraph, 7 words). Role qualifies.
results.corrected_extracted: Positive symptoms: SMD −0.01 (−0.13 to 0.11), I² 0% in Fig. 1; the authors read this as no difference. Editors' recalculation (Hedges' g, DerSimonian–Laird) from the means and dispersions in Table 1, reading those printed for Dawe 2011 and Hajebi 2018 as standard errors, as the review's own negative-symptom values in Fig. 2 require: −0.29 (−0.67 to 0.10), I² 89%, study values from −1.93 to 0.54 (taking every dispersion as an SD, as printed: −0.35, −0.90 to 0.20, I² 94%, study values from −1.98 to 1.20). None of the 12 study values in Fig. 1 (−0.19 to 0.15) is reproduced either way; for example Mikami 2003 (1.7 ± 2.1 vs 7.3 ± 3.8) appears as −0.04.

results.note: Table 1 (p. 185), the Hajebi reference title (p. 189), 2.4 (p. 183), 3.2 2nd paragraph (p. 184), 4.6 (p. 188) and the abstract all match. The mix of persistent psychosis and current use follows inclusion criterion d) rather than departing from it, so the sentence is split; numbers unchanged. Role qualifies.
results.corrected_extracted: Groups depart from the stated criteria: the primary psychotic disorder group in Hides 2015 (20 people) was drawn from 198 people who had used methamphetamine in the previous month; Hajebi 2018 compared first-episode primary psychosis (reference title) although first-episode psychosis was an exclusion criterion. The criteria themselves admit both persistent psychosis after recent cessation and psychosis with current use, so the methamphetamine-psychosis groups mix the two; six studies reported other substance use; the authors state that the cross-sectional designs allow no causal interpretation.

results.note: Table 1 rows (pp. 185–186) and reference entries (Chen 2015, p. 189; Wang 2016a, p. 190): the same seven authors in a different order; 56 vs 54 and 53 vs 53; negative 9.0 vs 10.5 and 9.1 vs 10.6; positive 17.0 vs 18.2 and 16.8 vs 18.2; chlorpromazine equivalents 1100 ± 600 vs 1200 ± 600 in both. The overlap is labelled as the editors' inference. Role qualifies.
